Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: BrickBench is a benchmark for evaluating agentic LEGO-set design, assessing agents' ability to create physically buildable assemblies from text prompts while meeting design criteria.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: ARC: A Reasoning Recipe for Robot Foundation Models
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Gokul Puthumanaillam, Tao Sun, Elie Aljalbout, Moritz Reuss, Zhaoshuo Li
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The ARC framework enhances robot foundation models' zero-shot performance through effective reasoning traces and automatic labeling, achieving unprecedented gains without additional training or demonstrations.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: The prevailing approach to improving robot foundation models (RFMs) relies on larger models, more robot demonstrations, and costly training at scale. We show that there exists an effective and efficient complementary approach: the right reasoning recipe can substantially improve the zero-shot task performance of existing state-of-the-art RFMs. We refer to this recipe as ARC. It consists of three key ingredients: a reasoning trace, a scalable automatic labeling pipeline, and a strategy for adapting pretrained RFMs to use these traces for control. First, we find that effective reasoning traces should be grounded in the robot's next action and explain its causal structure: why the action is appropriate and what effect it should produce. Second, we show that these traces can be generated automatically from existing demonstrations, enabling us to construct ARC-Trace-DROID from DROID without collecting new robot data. Third, we show how state-of-the-art VLAs such as $π_{0.5}$ and WAMs such as Cosmos3-Nano-Policy can learn to use these traces for control, with fine-tuning and inference tailored to each model's architecture and capabilities. Using ARC, we obtain gains in zero-shot RFM performance that, to our knowledge, are unprecedented without additional robot demonstrations or foundation-scale training. The adapted models establish a new state of the art on RoboLab-120 and MolmoSpaces, with gains of up to 50 percentage points on RoboLab-Reasoning-50. On real robots, ARC improves $π_{0.5}$'s task success by 82.2 percentage points. Project website: https://arc-robot-reasoning.github.io/

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: TouchScale: 500 Hours of Human Vision and Touch for Visual-Tactile Learning
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Qianqian Yang, Zihao Zhu, Haoquan Fang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: TouchScale is a 500-hour dataset of synchronized visual-tactile human interactions that significantly enhances robot manipulation and perception through large-scale, consistent data collection.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Large-scale egocentric human interaction data is becoming an important source of physical supervision for embodied learning, yet video alone leaves the contact and pressure that characterize physical interaction unrecorded. Recent visual-tactile datasets provide this missing supervision, but their synchronized tactile data remain far smaller in volume than human video. Moreover, the largest resources often merge recordings from different sensors or annotation procedures, which makes the effect of data scale difficult to isolate. We therefore introduce TouchScale, a 500-hour dataset of contact-rich human interaction recorded with a single unified wearable setup. Its approximately 2K predefined task descriptions span everyday activities and structured manipulation, and each recording temporally aligns egocentric RGB-D video with wrist RGB video and dense full-hand bimanual tactile measurements. Compared with prior tactile data, training on the full TouchScale raises zero-shot contact IoU on data from an unseen tactile sensor from 0.134 to 0.383. Pretraining a visual encoder on TouchScale also yields the highest action recognition accuracy on three benchmarks among the compared visual-tactile datasets. Used for visual-tactile mid-training of a robot policy, TouchScale improves the average real-world success rate across four contact-rich manipulation tasks from 22.5% to 57.5%. With the sensor and collection protocol held fixed, both zero-shot tactile prediction and robot success show an overall upward trend as more TouchScale data is used. These results suggest that human visual-tactile data collected at scale with consistent sensing benefits both perception and robot manipulation. We will publicly release TouchScale, including all synchronized visual-tactile recordings and reconstructed object models, to support future research on scalable visual-tactile learning.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Autogenesis: A Self-Evolving Agent Protocol
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Wentao Zhang, Zhe Zhao, Haibin Wen, Yingcheng Wu, Cankun Guo
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The Autogenesis Protocol (AGP) enables self-evolving agent systems to manage heterogeneous updates through a structured lifecycle, enhancing performance in various benchmarks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: LLM-based agent systems can adapt by revising prompts, constructing tools, and changing other runtime resources. Managing these heterogeneous updates requires a shared lifecycle for identifying targets, assessing candidates, and retaining accepted versions, complementing communication protocols such as A2A and MCP. We introduce AUTOGENESIS PROTOCOL (AGP), which decouples what evolves from how updates are proposed. Its Resource Substrate Protocol Layer (RSPL) represents prompts, agents, tools, environments, and memory as protocol-registered resources with explicit state and versioned interfaces. Its Self-Evolution Protocol Layer (SEPL) specifies candidate proposal, assessment, and commit, with auditable histories and support for restoring retained resource states. We instantiate AGP in AUTOGENESIS SYSTEM (AGS), a self-evolving multi-agent system that retrieves, instantiates, and refines resources during execution. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding benchmarks, AGS improves over its non-evolving configuration, and repeated reasoning runs report the accompanying output-token cost. Execution cases show a shared update lifecycle across all five resource types.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: PCAsplat: Gaussian Splatting with Local PCA Regularization
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Vitor Matias, Filipe Nascimento, Kiyohiro Nakayama, João Paulo Lima, Márcus Lobo
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: PCAsplat introduces a geometry-aware regularization for Gaussian splatting using local PCA, enhancing surface alignment and reducing floaters in 3D reconstruction from posed images.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Gaussian splatting has emerged as a flexible representation for 3D reconstruction from posed images. However, existing methods are optimized primarily using rasterization-based losses, which supervise a splat only when it contributes to sampled camera rays. Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to the sampled view therefore receive weak or no geometric gradients and may drift away from the underlying surface, producing undesired floaters. We introduce PCAsplat, a geometry-aware regularization framework for Gaussian splatting based on differentiable local principal component analysis (PCA). Our PCA regularizer acts directly on neighborhoods of Gaussian centers and can therefore update Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. We regularize the PCA eigenvalues to encourage Gaussians to move to the underlying surface with isotropic tangent-plane coverage. We also align each Gaussian normal with the PCA-estimated neighborhood normal to enforce consistent orientation. Experiments on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and NeRF Synthetic show that the splats produced by PCAsplat better approximate samples of the reference surface while substantially reducing undesired floaters. These surface-aligned splats enable downstream geometry-processing tasks, including point cloud segmentation, and direct Poisson reconstruction. Additionally, PCAsplat remains competitive under conventional novel view synthesis and mesh extraction tasks. Code will be released.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Huang Huang, Sriram Yenamandra, Arjun Majumdar, Elie Aljalbout, Tushar Nagarajan
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM) enhances cross-embodiment learning by utilizing a unified latent action space, outperforming traditional explicit action conditioning.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model's performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM's downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlight the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics. Project website: https://lacwm.github.io/

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Haoxiang Zhang, Qinglin Chen, Hiroaki Hayashi, Zhuofeng Li, Siming Zhang
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper introduces Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), enhancing reinforcement learning by using post-hoc experiences to improve foresight predictions, significantly boosting performance in reward-scarce environments.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce prospective learning, which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when 37--98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In the 2B setting, where 98% of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at 0.0% success, while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction.

Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).title: Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).authors_text: Megha Srivastava, Cedric Colas, Dorsa Sadigh, Jacob Andreas
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).summary: The paper presents Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), enhancing AI agents' interpretability and generalization by integrating linguistic rule generation with policy learning across diverse tasks.
Stanford AI Lab (SAIL).debug_abstract: Modern AI systems such as self-driving cars and game-playing agents can achieve superhuman performance, but often lack human-like generalization, interpretability, and inter-operability with human users. Inspired by the rich interactions between language and decision-making in humans, we introduce Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), a framework enabling AI agents to generate linguistic rules that capture the high-level strategies underlying rewarding behaviors. PLLB alternates between a *rule generation* step guided by language models, and an *update* step where agents learn new policies guided by rules, even when a rule is insufficient to describe an entire complex policy. Across five diverse tasks, including a two-player signaling game, maze navigation, image reconstruction, and robot grasp planning, we show that PLLB agents are not only able to learn more interpretable and generalizable behaviors, but can also share the learned rules with human users, enabling more effective human-AI coordination. We provide source code for our experiments at https://github.com/meghabyte/bottleneck .

CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.title: FAITH: Feasibility-Aware Safety-Filtered RL for High-Dimensional Systems
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.authors_text: Songyuan Zhang, Baljeet Singh, Sarthak Ranjeet Kaingade, Chuchu Fan, Bryan Trinh
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.summary: FAITH introduces a model-free, feasibility-aware safety-filtered reinforcement learning framework that optimizes task performance while ensuring high safety rates in complex systems.
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.debug_abstract: Safe reinforcement learning commonly places safety and task performance in the same policy objective, where they can introduce competing updates. Safety filters separate them at action execution, but classical designs require an analytic safety function and dynamics model, and standard minimal-intervention filters are myopic to long-horizon task return because they minimize only instantaneous action deviation. Hard projections are also undefined when no safe action exists. We present FAITH, a feasibility-aware, model-free framework that approximates the optimal state-action safety value and amortizes minimal-intervention filtering with a feedforward network. The task policy optimizes the task return through the filtered dynamics, which recovers the feasible constrained problem without a competing safety term in the task-policy update. When no action satisfies the learned safety condition, the same filter approaches the action with minimum predicted peak harm. On a double integrator example and a Safety Gym environment, FAITH achieves the highest return among methods with no feasible-start violations and matches the lowest harm from infeasible starts. On a 29-DoF humanoid, it reaches a 99.95% safety rate while retaining 97% of the unfiltered return in Walking-Avoid, and obtains the highest measured safety rate in Push-Avoid by learning to sacrifice balancing and fall away from the protected region. The same policies are also demonstrated on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid.

CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.title: Refine Connections, Close the Gap: A Reliable Enhancement Framework for Driving Scene Topology
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.authors_text: Xiaoqi Wang, Dingyi Zhaung, David Paz, Wenbin He, Yucai Bai
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.summary: The paper presents TopoEnhance, a framework that improves the reliability of driving scene topology by enhancing connectivity reasoning and producing robust discrete topology graphs.
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.debug_abstract: In autonomous driving, understanding scene topology - the connectivity between lanes and traffic elements - is critical for safe path planning and motion control. While current methods excel at detecting individual map elements, their connectivity reasoning often falls short of its theoretical potential, leaving a significant performance gap relative to the theoretical upper-bound achievable given the underlying detections. Furthermore, the decision-ready topology graphs passed to downstream tasks often remain unreliable. Current approaches typically derive connectivity by thresholding continuous topology scores; however, these scores often fail to reflect the true logical likelihood of connectivity, resulting in false positives or missing connections. Existing benchmarks further overlook this issue by primarily evaluating continuous metrics, rather than assessing the discrete connectivity required for decision-making. To bridge these gaps, we propose TopoEnhance, a novel topology enhancement framework designed to unlock the latent potential of existing methods and improve the reliability of decision-ready topology. We formulate topology enhancement as a denoising-based reconstruction process, where the model learns to recover structural consistency from stochastically corrupted ground-truth graphs. This formulation enables the model to resolve logical inconsistencies and rectify unreliable connections, producing robust discrete topology graphs that closely approach theoretical maximum performance. Extensive experiments across different baselines show that TopoEnhance consistently improves both continuous topology metrics (TOP score), and discrete connectivity measured by our adapted Topology Jaccard Similarity (TJS) metric. As a flexible, source-agnostic framework, TopoEnhance delivers substantial gains across diverse state-of-the-art baselines without requiring retraining.

CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.title: Census-Based Population Autonomy For Distributed Robotic Teaming
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.authors_text: Tyler M. Paine, Anastasia Bizyaeva, Michael R. Benjamin
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.summary: This paper presents a layered model for multi-robot autonomy using census-based decision-making and multi-objective optimization, validated through experiments in diverse marine scenarios.
CSAIL Embodied Intelligence Labs.debug_abstract: Collaborating teams of robots show promise due to their ability to complete missions more efficiently and with improved robustness, attributes that are particularly useful for systems operating in marine environments. A key issue is how to model, analyze, and design these multi-robot systems to realize the full benefits of collaboration, a challenging task since the domain of multi-robot autonomy encompasses both collective and individual behaviors. This paper introduces a layered model of multi-robot autonomy that uses the principle of census, or a weighted count of the inputs from neighbors, for collective decision-making about teaming, coupled with multi-objective behavior optimization for individual decision-making about actions. The census component is expressed as a nonlinear opinion dynamics model and the multi-objective behavior optimization is accomplished using interval programming. This model can be reduced to recover foundational algorithms in distributed optimization and control, while the full model enables new types of collective behaviors that are useful in real-world scenarios. To illustrate these points, a new method for distributed optimization of subgroup allocation is introduced where robots use a gradient descent algorithm to minimize portions of the cost functions that are locally known, while being influenced by the opinion states from neighbors to account for the unobserved costs. With this method the group can collectively use the information contained in the Hessian matrix of the total global cost. The utility of this model is experimentally validated in three categorically different experiments with fleets of autonomous surface vehicles: an adaptive sampling scenario, a high value unit protection scenario, and a competitive game of capture the flag.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The Autogenesis Protocol (AGP) enables self-evolving agent systems to manage heterogeneous updates through a structured lifecycle, enhancing performance in various benchmarks.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: LLM-based agent systems can adapt by revising prompts, constructing tools, and changing other runtime resources. Managing these heterogeneous updates requires a shared lifecycle for identifying targets, assessing candidates, and retaining accepted versions, complementing communication protocols such as A2A and MCP. We introduce AUTOGENESIS PROTOCOL (AGP), which decouples what evolves from how updates are proposed. Its Resource Substrate Protocol Layer (RSPL) represents prompts, agents, tools, environments, and memory as protocol-registered resources with explicit state and versioned interfaces. Its Self-Evolution Protocol Layer (SEPL) specifies candidate proposal, assessment, and commit, with auditable histories and support for restoring retained resource states. We instantiate AGP in AUTOGENESIS SYSTEM (AGS), a self-evolving multi-agent system that retrieves, instantiates, and refines resources during execution. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding benchmarks, AGS improves over its non-evolving configuration, and repeated reasoning runs report the accompanying output-token cost. Execution cases show a shared update lifecycle across all five resource types.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: PCAsplat: Gaussian Splatting with Local PCA Regularization
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Vitor Matias, Filipe Nascimento, Kiyohiro Nakayama, João Paulo Lima, Márcus Lobo
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: PCAsplat introduces a geometry-aware regularization for Gaussian splatting using local PCA, enhancing surface alignment and reducing floaters in 3D reconstruction from posed images.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Gaussian splatting has emerged as a flexible representation for 3D reconstruction from posed images. However, existing methods are optimized primarily using rasterization-based losses, which supervise a splat only when it contributes to sampled camera rays. Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to the sampled view therefore receive weak or no geometric gradients and may drift away from the underlying surface, producing undesired floaters. We introduce PCAsplat, a geometry-aware regularization framework for Gaussian splatting based on differentiable local principal component analysis (PCA). Our PCA regularizer acts directly on neighborhoods of Gaussian centers and can therefore update Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. We regularize the PCA eigenvalues to encourage Gaussians to move to the underlying surface with isotropic tangent-plane coverage. We also align each Gaussian normal with the PCA-estimated neighborhood normal to enforce consistent orientation. Experiments on DTU, Tanks and Temples, and NeRF Synthetic show that the splats produced by PCAsplat better approximate samples of the reference surface while substantially reducing undesired floaters. These surface-aligned splats enable downstream geometry-processing tasks, including point cloud segmentation, and direct Poisson reconstruction. Additionally, PCAsplat remains competitive under conventional novel view synthesis and mesh extraction tasks. Code will be released.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Huang Huang, Sriram Yenamandra, Arjun Majumdar, Elie Aljalbout, Tushar Nagarajan
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM) enhances cross-embodiment learning by utilizing a unified latent action space, outperforming traditional explicit action conditioning.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model's performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM's downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining. In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlight the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics. Project website: https://lacwm.github.io/

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Self-Retrospection Distillation: Turning Post-hoc Experiences into Prior Foresight
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Haoxiang Zhang, Qinglin Chen, Hiroaki Hayashi, Zhuofeng Li, Siming Zhang
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The paper introduces Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD), enhancing reinforcement learning by using post-hoc experiences to improve foresight predictions, significantly boosting performance in reward-scarce environments.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) turns agent experience into learning signals primarily through scalar outcome rewards after interaction. For group-relative objectives, however, this signal vanishes when all rollouts receive the same reward, even though their trajectories may reveal useful information about what the task requires and how the agent fails. We ask a complementary question: can hindsight teach an agent what it could have anticipated before acting? We introduce prospective learning, which uses post-hoc experience to supervise foresight predictions from the pre-interaction view, and instantiate it with Self-Retrospection Distillation (SRD). Intuitively, a completed trajectory reveals knowledge that would have been useful and pitfalls that should be avoided; SRD distills this privileged hindsight into trajectory-blind foresight of the same policy. Foresight serves only as a training target and need not be explicitly generated at inference time. Across 10 tool-integrated reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks, SRD complements RLVR and self-distillation baselines with gains of up to 24.2 pp. Its advantage is especially pronounced when reward contrast is scarce: when 37--98% of rollout groups are reward-uniform across model scales, yet SRD can still exploit learning signal from sampled trajectories. In the 2B setting, where 98% of groups are all-failure, the RLVR training ends up at 0.0% success, while adding SRD reaches 60.6% under the same rollout budget. Our results suggest that post-hoc agent experience is useful not only for evaluating or improving behavior, but also for shaping predictive representations before available interaction.

斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).title: Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).authors_text: Megha Srivastava, Cedric Colas, Dorsa Sadigh, Jacob Andreas
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).summary: The paper presents Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), enhancing AI agents' interpretability and generalization by integrating linguistic rule generation with policy learning across diverse tasks.
斯坦福-人工智能实验室 (SAIL).debug_abstract: Modern AI systems such as self-driving cars and game-playing agents can achieve superhuman performance, but often lack human-like generalization, interpretability, and inter-operability with human users. Inspired by the rich interactions between language and decision-making in humans, we introduce Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), a framework enabling AI agents to generate linguistic rules that capture the high-level strategies underlying rewarding behaviors. PLLB alternates between a *rule generation* step guided by language models, and an *update* step where agents learn new policies guided by rules, even when a rule is insufficient to describe an entire complex policy. Across five diverse tasks, including a two-player signaling game, maze navigation, image reconstruction, and robot grasp planning, we show that PLLB agents are not only able to learn more interpretable and generalizable behaviors, but can also share the learned rules with human users, enabling more effective human-AI coordination. We provide source code for our experiments at https://github.com/meghabyte/bottleneck .

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: BrickBench is a benchmark for evaluating agentic LEGO-set design, assessing agents' ability to create physically buildable assemblies from text prompts while meeting design criteria.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: ARC: A Reasoning Recipe for Robot Foundation Models
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Gokul Puthumanaillam, Tao Sun, Elie Aljalbout, Moritz Reuss, Zhaoshuo Li
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: The ARC framework enhances robot foundation models' zero-shot performance through effective reasoning traces and automatic labeling, achieving unprecedented gains without additional training or demonstrations.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: The prevailing approach to improving robot foundation models (RFMs) relies on larger models, more robot demonstrations, and costly training at scale. We show that there exists an effective and efficient complementary approach: the right reasoning recipe can substantially improve the zero-shot task performance of existing state-of-the-art RFMs. We refer to this recipe as ARC. It consists of three key ingredients: a reasoning trace, a scalable automatic labeling pipeline, and a strategy for adapting pretrained RFMs to use these traces for control. First, we find that effective reasoning traces should be grounded in the robot's next action and explain its causal structure: why the action is appropriate and what effect it should produce. Second, we show that these traces can be generated automatically from existing demonstrations, enabling us to construct ARC-Trace-DROID from DROID without collecting new robot data. Third, we show how state-of-the-art VLAs such as $π_{0.5}$ and WAMs such as Cosmos3-Nano-Policy can learn to use these traces for control, with fine-tuning and inference tailored to each model's architecture and capabilities. Using ARC, we obtain gains in zero-shot RFM performance that, to our knowledge, are unprecedented without additional robot demonstrations or foundation-scale training. The adapted models establish a new state of the art on RoboLab-120 and MolmoSpaces, with gains of up to 50 percentage points on RoboLab-Reasoning-50. On real robots, ARC improves $π_{0.5}$'s task success by 82.2 percentage points. Project website: https://arc-robot-reasoning.github.io/

Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.title: TouchScale: 500 Hours of Human Vision and Touch for Visual-Tactile Learning
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.authors_text: Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Qianqian Yang, Zihao Zhu, Haoquan Fang
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.summary: TouchScale is a 500-hour dataset of synchronized visual-tactile human interactions that significantly enhances robot manipulation and perception through large-scale, consistent data collection.
Robotics and Embodied Artificial Intelli.debug_abstract: Large-scale egocentric human interaction data is becoming an important source of physical supervision for embodied learning, yet video alone leaves the contact and pressure that characterize physical interaction unrecorded. Recent visual-tactile datasets provide this missing supervision, but their synchronized tactile data remain far smaller in volume than human video. Moreover, the largest resources often merge recordings from different sensors or annotation procedures, which makes the effect of data scale difficult to isolate. We therefore introduce TouchScale, a 500-hour dataset of contact-rich human interaction recorded with a single unified wearable setup. Its approximately 2K predefined task descriptions span everyday activities and structured manipulation, and each recording temporally aligns egocentric RGB-D video with wrist RGB video and dense full-hand bimanual tactile measurements. Compared with prior tactile data, training on the full TouchScale raises zero-shot contact IoU on data from an unseen tactile sensor from 0.134 to 0.383. Pretraining a visual encoder on TouchScale also yields the highest action recognition accuracy on three benchmarks among the compared visual-tactile datasets. Used for visual-tactile mid-training of a robot policy, TouchScale improves the average real-world success rate across four contact-rich manipulation tasks from 22.5% to 57.5%. With the sensor and collection protocol held fixed, both zero-shot tactile prediction and robot success show an overall upward trend as more TouchScale data is used. These results suggest that human visual-tactile data collected at scale with consistent sensing benefits both perception and robot manipulation. We will publicly release TouchScale, including all synchronized visual-tactile recordings and reconstructed object models, to support future research on scalable visual-tactile learning.

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Huang Huang, Sriram Yenamandra, Arjun Majumdar, Elie Aljalbout, Tushar Nagarajan

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model's performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results show that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots. We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. 斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Haoxiang Zhang, Qinglin Chen, Hiroaki Hayashi, Zhuofeng Li, Siming Zhang

斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).title: Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).authors_text: Megha Srivastava, Cedric Colas, Dorsa Sadigh, Jacob Andreas
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).summary: The paper presents Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), enhancing AI agents' interpretability and generalization by integrating linguistic rule generation with policy learning across diverse tasks.
斯坦福-视觉与学习实验室 (SVL).debug_abstract: Modern AI systems such as self-driving cars and game-playing agents can achieve superhuman performance, but often lack human-like generalization, interpretability, and inter-operability with human users. Inspired by the rich interactions between language and decision-making in humans, we introduce Policy Learning with a Language Bottleneck (PLLB), a framework enabling AI agents to generate linguistic rules that capture the high-level strategies underlying rewarding behaviors. PLLB alternates between a *rule generation* step guided by language models, and an *update* step where agents learn new policies guided by rules, even when a rule is insufficient to describe an entire complex policy. Across five diverse tasks, including a two-player signaling game, maze navigation, image reconstruction, and robot grasp planning, we show that PLLB agents are not only able to learn more interpretable and generalizable behaviors, but can also share the learned rules with human users, enabling more effective human-AI coordination. We provide source code for our experiments at https://github.com/meghabyte/bottleneck .

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: BrickBench: Evaluating Agentic Brick Design
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Peter Kulits, Yiqing Xu, R. Kenny Jones, Cordelia Schmid, Jiajun Wu
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: BrickBench is a benchmark for evaluating agentic LEGO-set design, assessing agents' ability to create physically buildable assemblies from text prompts while meeting design criteria.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: We propose BrickBench, a benchmark for agentic text-conditioned LEGO-set design. Given a prompt, an agent is tasked with producing an assembly that not only satisfies semantic and design criteria, but that can also be physically built. To do so, it must select parts from a discrete library and reason jointly about local and global constraints. We score validity, alignment, and design across three settings that vary in scale and part availability. We provide BrickAgent, an environment for coding agents to construct, inspect, and validate their designs. We find that leading agents largely satisfy verifiable physical and semantic requirements, but fall short of human designs. We release our benchmark and environment at http://www.brickben.ch

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: ARC: A Reasoning Recipe for Robot Foundation Models
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Gokul Puthumanaillam, Tao Sun, Elie Aljalbout, Moritz Reuss, Zhaoshuo Li
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The ARC framework enhances robot foundation models' zero-shot performance through effective reasoning traces and automatic labeling, achieving unprecedented gains without additional training or demonstrations.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: The prevailing approach to improving robot foundation models (RFMs) relies on larger models, more robot demonstrations, and costly training at scale. We show that there exists an effective and efficient complementary approach: the right reasoning recipe can substantially improve the zero-shot task performance of existing state-of-the-art RFMs. We refer to this recipe as ARC. It consists of three key ingredients: a reasoning trace, a scalable automatic labeling pipeline, and a strategy for adapting pretrained RFMs to use these traces for control. First, we find that effective reasoning traces should be grounded in the robot's next action and explain its causal structure: why the action is appropriate and what effect it should produce. Second, we show that these traces can be generated automatically from existing demonstrations, enabling us to construct ARC-Trace-DROID from DROID without collecting new robot data. Third, we show how state-of-the-art VLAs such as $π_{0.5}$ and WAMs such as Cosmos3-Nano-Policy can learn to use these traces for control, with fine-tuning and inference tailored to each model's architecture and capabilities. Using ARC, we obtain gains in zero-shot RFM performance that, to our knowledge, are unprecedented without additional robot demonstrations or foundation-scale training. The adapted models establish a new state of the art on RoboLab-120 and MolmoSpaces, with gains of up to 50 percentage points on RoboLab-Reasoning-50. On real robots, ARC improves $π_{0.5}$'s task success by 82.2 percentage points. Project website: https://arc-robot-reasoning.github.io/

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: TouchScale: 500 Hours of Human Vision and Touch for Visual-Tactile Learning
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Dayou Li, Hao Wang, Qianqian Yang, Zihao Zhu, Haoquan Fang
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: TouchScale is a 500-hour dataset of synchronized visual-tactile human interactions that significantly enhances robot manipulation and perception through large-scale, consistent data collection.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Large-scale egocentric human interaction data is becoming an important source of physical supervision for embodied learning, yet video alone leaves the contact and pressure that characterize physical interaction unrecorded. Recent visual-tactile datasets provide this missing supervision, but their synchronized tactile data remain far smaller in volume than human video. Moreover, the largest resources often merge recordings from different sensors or annotation procedures, which makes the effect of data scale difficult to isolate. We therefore introduce TouchScale, a 500-hour dataset of contact-rich human interaction recorded with a single unified wearable setup. Its approximately 2K predefined task descriptions span everyday activities and structured manipulation, and each recording temporally aligns egocentric RGB-D video with wrist RGB video and dense full-hand bimanual tactile measurements. Compared with prior tactile data, training on the full TouchScale raises zero-shot contact IoU on data from an unseen tactile sensor from 0.134 to 0.383. Pretraining a visual encoder on TouchScale also yields the highest action recognition accuracy on three benchmarks among the compared visual-tactile datasets. Used for visual-tactile mid-training of a robot policy, TouchScale improves the average real-world success rate across four contact-rich manipulation tasks from 22.5% to 57.5%. With the sensor and collection protocol held fixed, both zero-shot tactile prediction and robot success show an overall upward trend as more TouchScale data is used. These results suggest that human visual-tactile data collected at scale with consistent sensing benefits both perception and robot manipulation. We will publicly release TouchScale, including all synchronized visual-tactile recordings and reconstructed object models, to support future research on scalable visual-tactile learning.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: Autogenesis: A Self-Evolving Agent Protocol
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Wentao Zhang, Zhe Zhao, Haibin Wen, Yingcheng Wu, Cankun Guo
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: The Autogenesis Protocol (AGP) enables self-evolving agent systems to manage heterogeneous updates through a structured lifecycle, enhancing performance in various benchmarks.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: LLM-based agent systems can adapt by revising prompts, constructing tools, and changing other runtime resources. Managing these heterogeneous updates requires a shared lifecycle for identifying targets, assessing candidates, and retaining accepted versions, complementing communication protocols such as A2A and MCP. We introduce AUTOGENESIS PROTOCOL (AGP), which decouples what evolves from how updates are proposed. Its Resource Substrate Protocol Layer (RSPL) represents prompts, agents, tools, environments, and memory as protocol-registered resources with explicit state and versioned interfaces. Its Self-Evolution Protocol Layer (SEPL) specifies candidate proposal, assessment, and commit, with auditable histories and support for restoring retained resource states. We instantiate AGP in AUTOGENESIS SYSTEM (AGS), a self-evolving multi-agent system that retrieves, instantiates, and refines resources during execution. Across reasoning, tool-use, and coding benchmarks, AGS improves over its non-evolving configuration, and repeated reasoning runs report the accompanying output-token cost. Execution cases show a shared update lifecycle across all five resource types.

斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).title: PCAsplat: Gaussian Splatting with Local PCA Regularization
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).authors_text: Vitor Matias, Filipe Nascimento, Kiyohiro Nakayama, João Paulo Lima, Márcus Lobo
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).summary: PCAsplat introduces a geometry-aware regularization for Gaussian splatting using local PCA, enhancing surface alignment and reducing floaters in 3D reconstruction from posed images.
斯坦福-机器人与具身智能实验室 (REAL).debug_abstract: Gaussian splatting has emerged as a flexible representation for 3D reconstruction from posed images. However, existing methods are optimized primarily using rasterization-based losses, which supervise a splat only when it contributes to sampled camera rays. Gaussians that are occluded or contribute little to the sampled view therefore receive weak or no geometric gradients and may drift away from the underlying surface, producing undesired floaters. We introduce PCAsplat, a geometry-aware regularization framework for Gaussian splatting based on differentiable local principal component analysis (PCA). Our PCA regularizer acts directly on neighborhoods of Gaussian centers and can therefore update Gaussians that do not contribute to the current training view. We regularize the PCA eigenvalues to encourage Gaussians to move to the underlying surface with isotropic tangent-plane coverage. We also align each Gaussian normal with the PCA-estimated neighborhood normal to enforce consistent orientation. These surface-aligned splats enable downstream geometry-processing tasks, including point cloud segmentation, and direct Poisson reconstruction. Additionally, PCAsplat remains competitive under conventional novel view synthesis and mesh extraction tasks. Code will be released.
